Umicom · Learn by building

Create a drawing, a moving card and a short tune

Learn one editing workflow, then use it across Umicom’s creative applications. Start with a measured room plan, explore keyframes and notes, and export files you can open outside the workbench.

1. Start with one shared workbench

A drawing, an animation and a piece of music seem quite different. They still need some of the same things: a project name, a way to edit without losing earlier work, a saved version and a reliable export. The Umicom creative workbench supplies those common parts through Framework. The applications choose a starting project rather than each owning a different storage or editing engine.

You will begin with a small room layout in Kitchen Designer. Afterwards, the same controls will help you make a moving title card, a short note sequence and a visual page prototype. No programming knowledge is needed for the main lessons.

ApplicationStarting point in this workbench
CAD and Kitchen DesignerA measured, rectangular 2D plan in millimetres.
Media StudioA title and a card with position keyframes.
Music StudioA four-note sequence that can be rendered to WAVE.
GamesAn actor and a wall for a collision playground.
Web Studio and Mobile StudioA visual page layout that can be exported as standalone HTML.

Use Creative workbench to open these controls. Existing layouts keeps the application's earlier workspace available. The two pages are not two copies of your creative project.

What the lesson creates

These are small, editable designs and real exported files. A 2D plan is not a 3D CAD model or an approved construction drawing. The HTML is a visual prototype, not an installed mobile application. A storyboard is a set of frames, not encoded video.

2. Create a room project

Open Umicom Kitchen Designer. In a Windows source build, its executable is umicom-kitchen-designer.exe in build\windows-ucrt64-all-debug\bin. Open the Project tab of the creative workbench.

  1. Enter workshop-room as the Project ID. This is the short name used to find the project again. An ID may contain letters, digits, full stops, underscores and hyphens; it must start with a letter or digit.
  2. Enter Workshop room as the Project title. Unlike the ID, the title may contain spaces and Unicode text.
  3. Choose millimetres for the units. Set the width to 3000 and the height to 2400. Leave the duration at 8000 milliseconds and the tempo at 120. They will become useful in later lessons.
  4. Choose Create new project. Check the status message. Creating a project never overwrites an existing ID. When the ID is already in use, choose Open project by ID instead, or enter a different ID.
  5. Choose Load starter into empty project. The drawing now contains a base cabinet, a sink unit and a workshop table. The starter establishes the profile's canvas, units, duration and tempo. It will not replace a project that already contains objects or notes.

The storage line shows the resolved database path after it opens. The database belongs to the user's Umicom data directory, not the folder from which the application was launched. Opening the workbench alone does not create or open that database.

Check your result: the report should list cabinet, sink and table. The canvas measures 3000 by 2400 millimetres. The base cabinet is 600 by 600 millimetres.

Back to the contents

3. Move an object and try undo

The drawing uses a simple coordinate system. x measures distance from the left edge. y measures distance down from the top. Width and height describe the object's size in the project's units.

  1. Open Objects. Enter cabinet in Object ID and choose Load object into form. Clicking the cabinet on the drawing also loads it. When objects overlap, the topmost visible object is selected.
  2. Change Left (x) from 100 to 200. Nothing has been saved yet: you are editing a form, not the stored object.
  3. Choose Update object. The cabinet moves right and the saved project's revision increases. A revision is a sequence number for a successful saved change.
  4. Choose Undo. The cabinet returns to x = 100. Choose Redo to put it back at x = 200. Undo and redo are themselves saved changes, so the revision keeps increasing rather than going backwards.

At x = 200, the cabinet ends exactly where the sink begins: their edges touch, but their rectangular areas do not overlap. Try x = 250 and choose Update. The report now identifies an overlap. The drawing editor reports it instead of moving your objects without asking. Use Undo to return to the previous arrangement.

Add object requires a new ID. Update object requires an existing one. This distinction prevents a mistyped name from silently replacing something else. Send to back and Bring to front change the paint order. Hiding an object keeps it in the project while excluding it from the drawing and overlap report.

A failed edit leaves the saved project unchanged. For example, an object cannot extend beyond the canvas, and an animation cannot carry it beyond the canvas later. Read the status message, correct the form and try again.

Why is changing units restricted?

Changing “600 pixels” to “600 millimetres” is not a real conversion. To avoid relabelling an existing design by accident, the settings editor does not change units while objects remain in the project. Start a new project with the intended units.

Back to the contents

4. Reopen work and export a drawing

Every successful workbench edit is saved immediately. There is no separate “save everything later” button for these creative records. Form text that has not been submitted with Add, Update or Save is not part of the saved project.

  1. Open Export and choose SVG drawing. SVG stores the drawing as shapes and text rather than a fixed grid of pixels.
  2. Choose Suggest an output path. Inspect the full path. It includes the project ID and loaded revision, for example workshop-room-r5.svg. The revision may differ if you have made more edits.
  3. Choose Write a new export file. Open that file in a browser or another SVG viewer. A measured project includes its physical width and height in millimetres.
  4. Close Kitchen Designer, reopen it, enter workshop-room in Project ID and choose Open project by ID. The saved objects should return.

The exporter never overwrites an existing file. Choose another filename when a path already exists. A write failure can leave a newly created, incomplete file for inspection; it is not presented as a finished export. Nothing is deleted automatically.

You may open the same project in CAD or another creative application. The saved project keeps its units and contents; opening it does not replace it with the application's starter. After another application changes it, choose Reload saved project before editing your older copy. A stale edit is rejected rather than overwriting the newer work.

Saved work and undo history are different

The current design survives a restart. The last 16 undo steps belong to the current open workspace only. Reloading or reopening a project clears that local history; it does not erase the saved design.

5. Animate a title card

Open Media Studio, create a new project with ID workshop-card, then load its starter. The starter contains a heading and a card. Open Objects, enter card and load it.

A keyframe states where an object should be at a particular time. In this workbench, a key stores an offset from the object's saved left/top position. The card starts at (40, 180). An offset of (500, 100) therefore places it at (540, 280), not (500, 100).

TimeOffsetWhat follows this key
0 ms(0, 0)Linear movement towards the next key.
4000 ms(500, 100)Hold this position until the next key.
8000 ms(180, 0)The final position.
  1. Move the preview slider to 2000. Halfway through the first segment, the card is at (290, 230).
  2. Compare 4000 ms and 7000 ms. The card stays at (540, 280) because the segment is set to hold.
  3. Move to 8000 ms. At the exact final key, the card is at (220, 180).
  4. Open Motion. To try an extra key, keep Object ID set to card, enter time 1000, horizontal offset 100, vertical offset 40, and choose Linear movement. Choose Save or replace key at this time.

The first key must be at time zero. Saving a key at an existing time replaces that key, not the whole animation. The report lists the saved keys so you can inspect them before changing another one. Scrubbing the slider does not save a change.

Choose Three-frame storyboard in Export to make a standalone HTML page containing the start, midpoint and end. This is a useful way to share timing ideas without claiming that a video file has been rendered.

6. Turn notes into an audio file

Open Music Studio and create workshop-sound. Load its starter. The report lists four notes: C, E, G and a higher C. A pitch number selects the note; 69 is A4. Velocity controls a note's relative level.

Musical time uses ticks. There are 480 ticks in one beat. At 120 beats per minute, a beat lasts half a second. The starter's four 480-tick notes therefore last two seconds, followed by silence until the eight-second project ends.

  1. Open Notes. Enter a new Note ID, ending-a.
  2. Set Start tick to 1920, Length in ticks to 960, Pitch number to 69 and Velocity to 80.
  3. Choose Add note. The new note starts after the four starter notes and lasts two beats. The report shows its saved timing.
  4. Choose PCM-WAVE notes in Export, suggest a new path and write the file. Open the WAVE file in an audio player to listen.

The output is a real 48,000 Hz, mono, 16-bit PCM-WAVE file. The voice is a simple sine wave with short fades at its edges. Notes that overlap are mixed with headroom. This is a note renderer, not a microphone recorder, full synthesiser or audio-device engine.

Listen to the original four-note starter

This sample was generated by the delivered C example. It contains the original four notes, without the extra A from the exercise. Start playback yourself and set your player's volume as appropriate.

7. Try collision movement and page prototypes

A small collision playground

In Games, create workshop-game and load the starter. Load the object player in Objects. In Motion, choose Reset play position, then use the movement buttons.

The player begins at x = 40 and is 40 units wide. The wall begins at x = 260. Nine rightward moves of 20 units place the player at x = 220, where its right edge touches the wall. Another rightward move is blocked. Even a large requested movement through the developer API is checked across its entire distance; it cannot jump through a thin wall.

This movement is temporary. Reset returns to the saved position, and moving the player does not add undo steps or update the database. The playground accepts static rectangular scenes and one movement axis at a time. It is not a general physics engine. Use the report to distinguish a temporary play position from an actual design edit.

A visual page for different screen sizes

In Web Studio or Mobile Studio, create a fresh project and load its starter. Edit the panels and labels with the same Objects controls. Export Responsive visual page, then resize the browser window.

The saved drawing scales to the available width and the HTML includes a readable list of its objects. Mobile Studio begins with a narrower canvas, 360 by 640 pixels. The export does not send bookings, run JavaScript, fetch resources or produce an Android/iOS package. It lets you discuss the visual layout before implementing application behaviour.

8. Use the same services in a C application

The workbench is one client of the Framework services. Another Umicom application can use the same project, animation and export contracts without including GTK types in its domain logic.

The editing pattern is deliberate: copy the loaded state, change that copy, then submit the whole candidate with the revision you read. A failed validation or a conflicting writer leaves the saved state alone. The workspace borrows its Data Server, so destroy the workspace before destroying the server.

UmiCreativeProject *draft = calloc(1U, sizeof(*draft));
if (draft == NULL) return UMI_STATUS_OUT_OF_MEMORY;

UmiStatus status = UmiCreativeWorkspaceCopy(workspace, draft);
UmiCreativeElement table;
if (status == UMI_STATUS_OK) {
    status = UmiCreativeElementInit(&table, "table", "Workshop table",
        UMI_CREATIVE_RECTANGLE, 100, 100, 300, 150, 0x87A88BU);
}
if (status == UMI_STATUS_OK) {
    status = UmiCreativeProjectPutElement(draft, &table, false);
}
if (status == UMI_STATUS_OK) {
    status = UmiCreativeWorkspaceReplace(
        workspace, draft, draft->revision);
}
free(draft);
return status;

This fragment belongs inside a function whose caller already owns an open workspace. Include umicom/creative_workspace/workspace.h and stdlib.h. A complete executable example is supplied at framework/examples/creative_workspace_main.c.

The Master Controller composes the services. A creative Slave Controller can own the workspace's lifecycle and commands; its view receives copied project or frame values. GTK objects stay in the adapter. Persistence remains behind the Data Server, and the existing Framework animation track remains the sampler used by both the preview and exports.

Know the working limits

One project holds up to 48 objects, eight position keys per object and 64 notes. Duration is at most 30 seconds; tempo ranges from 20 to 300 BPM. Each canvas dimension is at most 1,000,000 units. Export buffers are limited to 4 MiB. The records are plaintext, so use non-sensitive design material. Undo stores 16 steps in the open workspace.

These limits are explicit so a caller receives an error rather than partial work. Larger projects, 3D solids, imported media assets, video encoding, recording, richer synthesis and application deployment need further services; changing a capacity constant alone does not implement those capabilities.

9. Build and test the workbench

These commands assume the Umicom source checkout and MSYS2 UCRT64 toolchain are already installed. Merge the supplied full files into their matching repository paths first. Keep your own uncommitted changes during the comparison; do not replace entire folders.

Configure and build

Set-Location "C:\umicom\Umicom-Applications"
$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"
$env:Path = "C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin;$env:Path"

& "C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin\cmake.exe" `
    --preset windows-ucrt64-all-debug `
    -DBUILD_TESTING=ON `
    -DUMICOM_BUILD_NATIVE_TOOL=ON
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "Configuration failed." }

& "C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin\cmake.exe" `
    --build `
    --preset windows-ucrt64-all-debug `
    --parallel 2 `
    -- -k 0
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "Build failed. Stop here." }

Run the complete test suite after the build succeeds

& "C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin\ctest.exe" `
    --preset windows-ucrt64-all-debug `
    --parallel 2 `
    --no-tests=error `
    --output-on-failure
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "Review the test failures." }

For a closer look at this workbench, add the selection below to a separate CTest run. It does not replace the full suite.

-R '^(framework\.creative_workspace\.|(media|music|cad|kitchen|games|web-studio|mobile-studio)\.creative_workspace\.)'

A skipped test is different from a passed test. For example, a graphical test may be skipped when no display is available. The independent export test uses Python 3 when CMake finds it. Check the configure output and the test summary rather than relying only on a percentage.

Run an example without changing files

& ".\build\windows-ucrt64-all-debug\bin\umicom-kitchen-creative-workspace-example.exe"
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "The example failed." }

The example creates a memory-only project and renders an export into memory. It does not write that export unless you explicitly supply --export, a format and a new absolute file path. The Music example renders its note sequence without opening an audio device.

After validation, commit and push Framework first, then each changed application module, and update the parent repository's lock and pins last. The delivery's merge instructions provide those commands. Do not commit unrelated work or secrets merely because a command uses git add -A.

10. Check what you have learned

Try these small exercises with a separate practice project. They are intended to make the behaviour visible, not to test how many button names you can remember.

  1. Make two rectangles touch at their edges. Move one a little further. What changes in the overlap report?
  2. Type a different position without choosing Update. Export the drawing. Which position appears, and why?
  3. Undo a saved edit, then make a different edit. Can you redo the discarded path?
  4. Put a held key between two other keys. Compare the moment just before it with its exact timestamp.
  5. At 120 BPM, place a note at tick 960 with a length of 480 ticks. When should it start and stop?
Compare your answers

Touching edges are not overlapping areas. An export uses the loaded saved project, not unsubmitted form text. A new edit after Undo starts a new history path and clears Redo. An exact key timestamp uses that key's value; the preceding held segment no longer applies. Tick 960 is two beats, so the note starts at one second and lasts half a second.

Once those results feel predictable, change the design's colours, labels and timing. The important habit is to keep the editable form, the saved project, the sampled preview and the exported file distinct. That habit applies to every application built from these Framework services.
